items.text: You didn't regress. You ran out of resources. The skills are still there — the capacity to run them isn't. Burnout isn't going backward. It's what happens when the external load was never sustainable.
items.rationale: Opens on the shame the community actually carries — 'regression' — and immediately flips it in two moves: the skills survived, the support system didn't. Closes by placing responsibility on external demands, not the person.

items.text: 'Regression' was borrowed from child development. It was never the right word for what autistic adults experience in burnout. Fluctuating capacity puts the blame where it belongs — on unsustainable demands.
items.rationale: Sibling to post 1 but leads with the linguistic argument — useful for people who want to push back on clinical framing with clinicians or employers. Stands fully alone.

items.text: The dominant story is: unmask and you'll feel free. What people don't say: after decades of masking to survive, the self underneath is unknown and unprotected. That can feel more like danger than liberation.
items.rationale: Leads with the public narrative before naming the honest experience. The contrast earns the point without invalidating hope — it makes room for a reality many people have never seen said aloud.

items.text: Unmasking isn't always relief. For a lot of late-diagnosed people it's disorienting — you masked so long you no longer know what's mask and what's you. That's not failure. That's identity reconstruction.
items.rationale: More intimate than post 3 — second-person, focused on the disorientation of not knowing your own self rather than the fear of exposure. Different angle on the same source material; stands alone.
items.sensitivity_flag: Source returned 403 on direct fetch — paraphrase only; verify wording before publishing.

items.text: PDA isn't willful defiance. It's an involuntary threat response. The nervous system treats loss of autonomy as equivalent to physical danger. That's not a character flaw. It's not even a choice.
items.rationale: Three declarative moves: name what it isn't, name what it is, strip the moral weight. Short rhythm mirrors the directness the voice guide calls for. Useful for adults explaining their experience to others.

items.text: If you can't feel 'tired' until you're already flattened, you can't pace. That's not laziness. That's the interoception gap — and it's why 'rest when you're tired' is functionally inaccessible advice.
items.rationale: Single causal mechanism: if the signal doesn't arrive reliably, the strategy built on that signal fails. Names the gap without overpromising a fix — keeps it honest to the research and opens space for follow-up conversation.

items.text: Self-care becomes avoidance bait the moment your brain tags it as an obligation. The fix isn't willpower — it's de-demanding the task. No deadline, free sequence, indirect framing. Works with the avoidance, not against it.
items.rationale: Names the mechanism then pivots immediately to concrete strategy. 'De-demanding' is doing real work — specific enough to be useful, open enough not to prescribe one exact solution.

items.text: Demand avoidance doesn't care that you want to do the thing. It fires on the structure of the demand, not its content. Showering, eating, hobbies — anything can get tagged. That's not a character issue.
items.rationale: Companion to post 7 but focused on recognition, not strategy — useful for people who haven't yet named the mechanism. The list makes it concrete fast. 'Character issue' closes the loop on the shame.
items.sensitivity_flag: Source returned 403 on direct fetch — verify framing before publishing.

items.text: 56% of managers say they lack the confidence to support neurodivergent colleagues. What does your workplace actually have — beyond a policy on the intranet?
items.rationale: The stat does the setup; the question invites honest, grounded replies rather than outrage. 'Beyond a policy on the intranet' names a real gap without accusing anyone personally. High relevance for late-diagnosed adults navigating accommodation conversations.
items.sensitivity_flag: Stat from NeuroBridge 2026 report — verify exact figure is 56% before publishing.

items.text: Neurodiversity tribunal claims are up 164% in four years. So what changed — the people, or the gap between what organisations promise and what they actually build?
items.rationale: The rhetorical question makes the argument without stating it: nothing changed about the people. More pointed than post 9 but earns it — the stat is the proof, and the framing is fair rather than hostile.
items.sensitivity_flag: Stat from NeuroBridge 2026 report — verify 164% figure and four-year window before publishing.

items.text: AuDHD isn't just having two things. It's two systems actively in conflict. Autistic nervous system craves routine; ADHD brain demands novelty. No clean rest strategy exists because rest from one is deprivation for the other.
items.rationale: The routine/novelty contrast does the work before the payoff line. Validates why every standard self-regulation script feels like it only half-applies — which is what AuDHD people actually live with, not just a sum of two profiles.
items.sensitivity_flag: Routine/novelty framing is a generalisation of common AuDHD experience, not universal — if tightening, 'many AuDHD people find' rather than absolute phrasing reduces overgeneralisation risk.

items.text: Late diagnosis isn't finding out you were broken. It's realising you spent decades navigating with a map made for different terrain. Every dead end makes sense now. You weren't lost — you had the wrong map.
items.rationale: The map metaphor holds both relief and grief in one image without naming either word. The closing line is the quotable payoff. Evergreen framing — defensible from lived-experience discourse, no stat required.
